clinicalPearls: Presents at birth with widespread erythroderma, superficial blistering and skin fragility, evolving into a chronic hyperkeratotic phenotype
Older children and adults show thick, ridged, often verrucous ('corrugated') hyperkeratosis, most marked in the flexures
A characteristic malodour and a tendency to recurrent bacterial skin infection accompany the hyperkeratosis
Caused by dominant mutations in the suprabasal keratins KRT1 or KRT10; KRT1 mutations tend to involve the palms and soles
The histological hallmark is epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (vacuolar degeneration of the upper epidermis with clumped keratin)
An epidermal naevus with the same histology can occur; if it involves the gonads, offspring may inherit generalised disease (mosaicism)
Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics, oral retinoids in severe cases, and antiseptic/antimicrobial measures for infection and odour
reference.pathophysiology: Epidermolytic ichthyosis is usually an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in KRT1 or KRT10, which encode the suprabasal keratins K1 and K10 that pair to form the intermediate-filament cytoskeleton of differentiating keratinocytes in the spinous and granular layers. The mutations, typically in conserved helix-boundary regions, exert a dominant-negative effect that destabilises the keratin network, so suprabasal keratinocytes cannot withstand mechanical stress and undergo cytolysis, producing blistering and the histological picture of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. Compensatory hyperproliferation and abnormal cornification yield the thick hyperkeratosis of later life, while barrier disruption predisposes to bacterial colonisation, infection and odour. Postzygotic mutation can produce a mosaic epidermal naevus with the same histology and a risk of transmitting generalised disease if gonadal tissue is involved.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital ichthyoses (lamellar ichthyosis, congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma)
Superficial epidermolytic ichthyosis (ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens, KRT2)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (vacuolar/reticular degeneration with clumped tonofilaments)
Molecular genetic testing of KRT1 and KRT10 (and KRT2 for the superficial variant)
Microbiological swabs of eroded or malodorous skin
Assessment of palmoplantar involvement to help localise the mutation (KRT1 vs KRT10)
Neonatal monitoring of fluid balance, temperature and infection
Family history and pedigree analysis, with counselling regarding mosaic naevi
redFlags: Neonatal barrier failure with dehydration, temperature instability or sepsis
Extensive erosions with fluid and electrolyte loss
Severe hyperkeratosis causing fissuring, pain or functional impairment
reference.prognosis: The neonatal blistering phase carries risks of infection and fluid loss but usually gives way to a chronic, stable hyperkeratotic phenotype compatible with a normal lifespan. The condition is lifelong and not curable; hyperkeratosis, odour and recurrent infection require ongoing management, and oral retinoids can help but may increase skin fragility.
pitfalls: Mistaking neonatal blistering for epidermolysis bullosa or staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Overusing keratolytics or high-dose retinoids that aggravate erosions and fragility
Neglecting antimicrobial care, so recurrent infection and malodour persist
Failing to counsel that a localised epidermolytic naevus may transmit generalised disease through gonadal mosaicism
